# Leading digits

## Leading digits of card purchases

*Do card purchase amounts follow Benford's law, and where do they depart from it?*

| First digit | Observed share | Benford's law | Interval |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | 30% | 30% | 95% CI 29% to 31% |
| 2 | 18% | 18% | 95% CI 17% to 19% |
| 3 | 11% | 12% | 95% CI 10% to 12% |
| 4 | 10% | 9.7% | 95% CI 9.3% to 11% |
| 5 | 7.2% | 7.9% | 95% CI 6.6% to 7.7% |
| 6 | 5.6% | 6.7% | 95% CI 5.2% to 6.0% |
| 7 | 5.7% | 5.8% | 95% CI 5.2% to 6.1% |
| 8 | 4.3% | 5.1% | 95% CI 3.9% to 4.6% |
| 9 | 8.4% | 4.6% | 95% CI 7.1% to 9.8% |

The mean absolute deviation from Benford's law is 0.0097
(95% CI 0.0082 to 0.013), which Nigrini's bands read as
**acceptable conformity**. The share of leading nines differs from the
law's expectation by +3.8 percentage points
(95% CI +2.5 to +5.2 points),
the usual mark of prices set just below a round number. The chi-square statistic is
535.5 (p < 0.001);
with this many amounts a rejection says more about the sample size than about the amounts.

Context: n = 515 clients, 14,496 events; 2023-10-02 to 2024-10-02; real extract, allow-listed aggregate; data fingerprint 85887a44d747.

Method: First significant digit of every positive card purchase amount (int_events, physical merchants, exact repeats excluded) against Benford's law: mean absolute deviation with Nigrini's conformity bands, chi-square test, and the excess of leading nines; client bootstrap intervals.

Caveats:

- With thousands of amounts the chi-square test rejects for tiny deviations; the MAD band is the recommended reading.
- Prices are set, not drawn: amounts just under a round number produce an excess of leading nines (psychological pricing), which is not a sign of manipulation.
